title: Agent tools
description: How an agent takes action: how the model calls tools and gets the results back.

steps.text: On its own, a model can do only one thing: write text. It can't open a file, set a reminder or look at a calendar. To do anything in the real world, it needs tools.

steps.imagePrompt: A glowing speech bubble with a friendly face floats in the center. Thin mechanical arms reach out from it toward everyday objects around it: an alarm clock, a paper calendar, a file folder, an envelope and a notification bell.
steps.caption: The model only writes text. Tools give it hands

steps.text: A tool is an action the model can ask to have done. In the lesson on the agent loop there was an “act” step. That step is a tool call. The model doesn't do the action itself. It asks the app.

steps.definition: An action the model can ASK for but can't do itself. The model asks, the app carries it out and returns the result to the conversation.
steps.example: “Set an alarm for 7:00”: the model names the tool and the time, the app sets the alarm, the model learns “done,” and only then answers you.

steps.text: It looks like this: the model decides an action is needed and names a tool with parameters, for example “set an alarm for 7:00.” The app makes the call and returns the result to the conversation.

steps.caption: Pick a time and run the call with the button: the model asks → the app does it → the model answers

steps.text: Note that the model doesn't pick out of thin air. It is shown a list of available tools in advance, with a description of what each one does and what parameters it takes. It picks the one that fits the task, the way you pick an app for a job. In this app, Muse Spark works this way: it is given the tool descriptions and decides which one to call. This is called function calling.

steps.caption: The model asks for a tool → the app runs it → the result goes back to the model

steps.text: Let's play one call through from start to finish. You write: “save to a file: buy milk.” The model replies, not to you but to the app: tool file_tool, action write_file, text “buy milk.” The app writes the file into the agent's folder and returns “file written.” The model sees that, and only now writes to you: “saved!”

steps.label: One call, part by part: “save to a file: buy milk”

parts.note: picked from the list of available ones
the result goes back into the conversation
the answer is written AFTER the result

steps.text: An agent has a wide set: files, memory, notifications and reminders, a calendar and an alarm, an email draft, a step counter, background tasks. These are essentially the agent's hands. Each tool gives it one specific ability.

pairs.def: wake you at the right moment
look at what you have today
get the step count from the device

steps.text: After it gets a result, the model doesn't stop. It reads the result and decides what's next: call another tool or answer you. That's how simple calls add up to real work, step by step.

One more thing: some tools need an Android permission, for example the calendar or notifications. You grant it once in the system, and without it the tool just returns an error. This is not the same as an “OK” for one specific action. Confirming risky calls is covered in a separate lesson.

A common misconception: “the model browses the internet and my files by itself.” It doesn't. The model only asks. The app always carries it out, and the app also decides what is allowed. Tools are the boundary of what an agent can do.

steps.question: And what if a tool returns an error, such as “file not found”?
steps.answer: That is a result too, and it goes back to the model. The model reads it and decides what to do: try another name, use another tool, or tell you honestly that it didn't work. A tool error doesn't crash the turn. It is just the next observation.

steps.text: This gives the first rule for agent builders: an agent is only as strong as its tools. Give it too few and it is helpless. Give it many with vague descriptions and it gets confused and calls the wrong one.

Tools also differ in how dangerous they are. Some only read. Others write, send data outside, or delete for good. An agent may read and write on its own, but the app won't let it send anything outside or delete anything without your “OK.” How this works, with risk classes, the confirmation bar and hooks, is covered in the lesson on tool approval.

Practice. After the lesson, ask me in an ordinary chat to do something with my hands, like “set an alarm for 7:00” or “remind me in 5 minutes to drink water,” and tap the wrench icon in the chat header. In the “Tool calls” panel you'll see which tool and which action I called and how it ended: “ok” or “error.”

In short. The model doesn't act, it asks: it writes a tool call with parameters. The app carries it out, the result returns to the conversation, and the loop goes on. The model gets the list of tools with descriptions in advance, and the limit of what it can do is its tools.

questions.q: What does “the model called a tool” mean?
options: It asked the app to perform an action and is waiting for the result; it doesn't do the action itself
It changes files and device settings directly, without asking the app
It invented and wrote a brand-new tool in the middle of its answer
questions.explain: The model only asks for an action with parameters. The app carries it out and returns the result.

questions.q: How does the model know which tools it has?
options: It is shown a list of tools in advance, with descriptions and parameters
It tries names at random until one of them works
The user dictates the list by hand at the start of every chat
questions.explain: The catalog of tools with descriptions is given to the model in advance, and it picks the one that fits.

questions.q: What usually happens after a tool returns a result?
options: The model reads the result and decides: call another tool or answer you
The conversation ends at once; after a tool the model stays silent
The result is sent straight to the cloud and stored there without the model
questions.explain: That is the loop: the result goes back to the model, and it decides the next step.
